guideTitle: The Best Drawing Tablets for a $100 Budget: One Screen Option and Seven Pen Pads
breadcrumbLabel: Best Drawing Tablets With Screens Under $100
metaTitle: Best Drawing Tablets With Screens Under $100: What Fits (2026)
metaDescription: An entry pen display sits just above $100; screenless tablets fit well below it. We compared both on drawing area, pen, shortcut keys and device compatibility.
introParagraphs: A $100 budget gets close to a drawing tablet with a screen, but not quite there in this guide. The 11.6-inch VEIKK VK1200 V2, the only pen display here, was listed at about $143 at the time of writing, and larger brand-name pen displays cost more again.

Everything else here is a screenless pen tablet, and all of them cost well under $100. You draw on a pad and watch the monitor, which takes some adjustment, but it leaves room in the budget for a larger pad or a better-known brand.

The practical question is whether a screen is worth stretching roughly $40 to $45 beyond budget, or whether a screenless tablet covers what you need. Our comparison is based on published specifications and listed compatibility, not hands-on testing.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: The only tablet here with a built-in screen: 11.6 inches, laminated, with a tilt-capable pen, at about $143.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
The VEIKK VK1200 V2 is the pick if drawing directly on a screen is non-negotiable, but it sits above a $100 budget: it was listed at about $143 at the time of writing.

VEIKK lists an 11.6-inch fully laminated display with anti-glare glass, and a battery-free pen with tilt support and 16,384 pressure levels. Lamination reduces the gap between pen tip and image, which is the main thing that makes a pen display feel direct.

A pen display also needs cable connections to your computer and desk space for the screen itself. If the budget is fixed, any of the screenless tablets below does the same basic job for a fraction of the price.
specs: Display: 11.6" fully laminated, anti-glare glass (per manufacturer)
cons: Above the $100 budget at the time of writing
Needs cable connections and more desk space
Listing gives few display details beyond size
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.bestFor: Anyone set on drawing directly on a screen who can stretch past $100.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.skipIf: Your $100 limit is firm; a screenless tablet such as the Wacom Intuos Small or the 10 x 6-inch Graphics Drawing Tablet fits it with room to spare.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: A very thin, light entry tablet with a battery-free 8,192-level pen, for the lowest price here.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
The HUION H420X is the least expensive way to try pen input: a 7mm-thick, 167g tablet with a battery-free pen offering 8,192 pressure levels.

HUION lists a 300 pps report rate and compatibility with Windows 7 or later, macOS 10.12 or later and Android 6.0 or later. Its small size makes it easy to carry and to fit beside a keyboard.

That size is also its limit: a small drawing area means shorter strokes map across the whole screen, which can feel twitchy on a large monitor. It suits signatures, note markup and first experiments more than extended illustration.
pros: Lowest price here at the time of writing
Works with Android as well as computers
cons: Small drawing area
No screen
Active area not stated in the listing summary
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.bestFor: Trying digital drawing or marking up documents for as little as possible.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.skipIf: You plan to draw regularly on a large monitor; a larger pad like the UGEE M708 gives more room.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: Wacom's small EMR tablet with a battery-free pen, from the brand with the most established drivers.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
The Wacom Intuos Small is the choice if you want the most established brand and drivers within budget. It uses Wacom's EMR battery-free pen technology, which Wacom describes as feeling like pen on paper.

Wacom says it works with any software program, for drawing, photo and video editing, design and document markup. Its practical advantage is the maturity of Wacom's driver support rather than a longer spec sheet.

Like the H420X, it is a small tablet, and it costs more than several larger alternatives here. If you want the most drawing area for the money, a UGEE or XOPPOX pad offers more.
specs: Software: works with common creative and office apps (per Wacom)
cons: Small drawing area for the price
No screen
Listing summary gives few measurable specs
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.bestFor: Beginners and students who value dependable drivers over drawing area.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.skipIf: You want the largest drawing area for the money; the 10 x 6-inch Graphics Drawing Tablet listing costs about $10 more.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: A larger ambidextrous pad with a passive pen, a pen holder and spare tips.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
The UGEE M708 is the better fit if you want more room to draw: UGEE describes a large active drawing space and an ambidextrous design for left- and right-handed users, with a pen holder and extra pen tips included.

The listing mentions 16,384-level passive stylus technology and compatibility with multiple operating systems and applications.

Other M708 listings in this guide cite 8,192 pressure levels, so confirm the pen specification on the listing you buy from. Its larger size also takes more desk space than the HUION or Wacom.
specs: Active area: large (exact size listed on the product page)
Pen: passive, battery-free; 16,384 levels per this listing
Design: ambidextrous, pen holder and spare tips
pros: More drawing room than the small tablets
Pen holder and spare tips included
cons: Pressure-level figure conflicts with other M708 listings
Takes more desk space
No screen
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.bestFor: Drawing on a large monitor, where a bigger pad makes strokes feel more controlled.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.skipIf: Your desk is crowded; the HUION H420X or H640P takes far less room.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: Another UGEE pen tablet listing that references the M708 pen and wide OS compatibility.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
This UGEE listing is hard to separate from the M708: its specifications reference the M708's pen and list compatibility with Windows 7 through 11 and other operating systems.

It was priced within a few dollars of the M708 at the time of writing, and the listing summary gives no size or pressure figures of its own.

We would treat it as an alternative listing rather than a distinct choice: compare both UGEE pages and buy whichever shows the configuration you want at the lower price.
specs: Size and pressure levels: check the listing
cons: Few specifications in the listing summary
Appears to overlap with the M708
No screen
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.bestFor: Readers comparing UGEE listings for the best price on the same class of tablet.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.skipIf: You want clear, published specifications; the UGEE M708 or Graphics Drawing Tablet listing states more.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: A compact 6 x 4-inch tablet with six customizable press keys and wide OS support.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
The HUION Inspiroy H640P is the pick if you want shortcut keys on a compact pad: six customizable press keys can be set to undo, zoom, brush switch or save, so your hand stays on the tablet.

It uses HUION's battery-free PW100 pen with 8,192 pressure levels, and HUION lists support for Mac, Windows, Linux and Android 6.0 or later.

At 6 x 4 inches, it is small, similar in role to the Wacom Intuos Small, and it costs little more than the H420X, which lacks the keys.
pros: Low price at the time of writing
cons: Small 6 x 4-inch area
No screen
Keys add less if you rarely use shortcuts
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.bestFor: Photo editing or drawing where quick undo and brush changes save time.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.skipIf: You need a larger drawing area; the Graphics Drawing Tablet listing offers 10 x 6 inches.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: A battery-free 8,192-level pen tablet with shortcut keys and listed support for Office apps.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
The XOPPOX tablet leans toward office use: XOPPOX lists compatibility with Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint alongside drawing apps, which suits annotation and handwritten notes on a work computer.

It has a battery-free pen with 8,192 pressure levels and shortcut keys, and supports Windows XP through 11, Android 4.4 and later, and macOS 11 or later.

The listing states it is not compatible with iPhone, iPad or Chromebook, so check your devices first. It is a smaller brand than HUION, Wacom or UGEE.
specs: Not compatible: iPhone, iPad, Chromebook (per listing)
cons: No iPad, iPhone or Chromebook support
Smaller brand
No screen
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.bestFor: Annotating documents and presentations on a Windows or Mac work computer.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.skipIf: You use a Chromebook; the Graphics Drawing Tablet listing supports Chrome OS 88 or later.

best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.summary: A 10 x 6-inch tablet with a tilt-capable pen, Chrome OS support and a full accessory kit.
best-drawing-tablets-with-screens-under-.description:
This Graphics Drawing Tablet listing, which describes a UGEE M708, offers the largest stated active area here at 10 x 6 inches, plus the most complete kit: a pen stand, eight replacement nibs, a nib ring, a two-finger glove, a cleaning brush and a cloth.

The listing describes a papery-textured surface and a tilt-supporting pen with 8,192 pressure levels, and compatibility with Windows 7 to 11, macOS 10.10 or later, Chrome OS 88 or later and Linux.

It is the most expensive screenless tablet here at the time of writing, though still about half the $100 budget. If you don't need the extras or Chromebook support, the UGEE M708 listing is cheaper.

Included: pen stand, 8 nibs, glove, cleaning brush and cloth
pros: Chrome OS and Linux support listed

buyingCriteria.criterion: Decide whether you really need a screen
buyingCriteria.explanation: A pen display lets you draw on the image; a screenless tablet asks you to look at the monitor while drawing on the pad. In this guide, the one screen tablet sits above $100 at the time of writing, while every screenless tablet costs less than $50.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Match the pad size to your monitor
buyingCriteria.explanation: A small pad mapped to a large monitor turns short hand movements into long cursor movements. If you draw on a large screen, a 10 x 6-inch pad is likely to feel more controlled than a 6 x 4-inch one.
Support differs: some tablets here list Android or Linux, one lists Chrome OS, and the XOPPOX excludes iPad, iPhone and Chromebook. Check your exact operating system version against the listing.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Treat pressure levels as a secondary number
buyingCriteria.explanation: Every pen here has at least 8,192 pressure levels listed. Beyond that, pad size, shortcut keys and driver support make a bigger practical difference.

faq.q: Can you buy a drawing tablet with a screen for under $100?
faq.a: Not among the tablets in this guide. The only screen tablet here, the VEIKK VK1200 V2, was about $143 at the time of writing. Under $100, the options here are screenless pen tablets.

faq.q: Is a screenless tablet hard to learn?
faq.a: It takes some adjustment, because you draw on the pad while looking at the monitor. Many artists work this way; how quickly you adapt varies from person to person.
The pens listed here are described as battery-free, so they don't need charging or batteries.

faq.q: Will these work with a Chromebook or iPad?
faq.a: Check each listing. The Graphics Drawing Tablet lists Chrome OS 88 or later; the XOPPOX states it is not compatible with iPhone, iPad or Chromebook.
All pens here list at least 8,192 levels. Above that, the difference is less significant than pad size, driver quality and whether the tablet has shortcut keys you'll use.

bottomLine: If you want to draw directly on a screen, the VEIKK VK1200 V2 is the option here, at roughly $40 to $45 over a $100 budget at the time of writing. If the budget is firm, a screenless tablet is the practical choice, and every one here leaves money to spare.

Among those, the 10 x 6-inch Graphics Drawing Tablet listing offers the largest area and the fullest kit, the Wacom Intuos Small the most established drivers, and the HUION H640P shortcut keys on a compact pad. The HUION H420X is the lowest-cost way to try pen input at all.
